To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have established a new cell culture model that can amplify HBV from clinical isolates and that this model can be used to study the spread of HBV in the infected liver and the response to antiviral therapy.

a slowly dividing liver cell line was selected that supports the entire HBV life cycle and efficiently produces and releases viral progeny, and that HBV derived from infected patients or cell cultures can be propagated in this system for long periods.
we developed an in vitro model of HBV infection that is able to replicate the virus and spread it between cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the establishment of an efficient HBV infection model for antiviral drug testing.
the development of an in vitro infection model that can be used for the evaluation of novel antiviral drugs and the study of HBV pathogenesis.
the improvement of HBV therapy and the development of novel antiviral drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this new model system is a useful tool to study the complete HBV replication cycle and the spread of HBV through the infected liver.
the new HepG2 NTPCsec+ cell line is a valuable model system for the study of HBV infection and antiviral drug resistance, as well as for the development of new antiviral drugs.
the novel HBV susceptible HepG2 NT CPsec+ cells efficiently spread HBV derived from clinical specimens or cell culture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a novel cell culture system for efficient amplification of HBB derived from patients or in vitro.

we have developed an efficient in vitro model for HBV infection and replication, which can be used to study the mechanisms of viral replication and spread in infected patients and to test the sensitivity of HBV to new antiviral drugs.
we developed a new cell model that can be used to investigate the dynamics of hepatitis virus spread in the liver.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a slowly dividing HepG2 cell line can support the entire HBV life cycle and long term viral spread.
this new infection model will allow the study of HBV spread and amplification from patient sera and the development of new antiviral therapies.
the cell culture model is able to reproduce the natural dynamics of HBV spread and amplification.
